name: Klickton Divide (via Warm Lake)
best_season: Mid-July through September, once the snow patch above Warm Lake has softened or melted; October and November ascents exist but need snow travel.
overview: The east-side way up the highest peak of the Goat Rocks. A long forest and meadow walk up the South Fork Tieton valley leads to Warm Lake, then a short climb gains the Klickton Divide, a broad ridge you follow west to the summit block. The finish is a short Class 3 scramble through a notch in the rock. It is usually done as a long day or an overnight at Warm Lake.
approach: Start at the Conrad Meadows trailhead at the end of the South Fork Tieton road (about 4,100 ft). Take the South Fork Tieton trail past Surprise Lake and on up the valley to the upper meadows near 5,900-6,000 ft where trails cross. Take the west branch and then the faint, unofficial path that reaches Warm Lake. Expect roughly 9-10 miles each way with about 4,200-4,600 ft of gain for the whole climb.
beta: From Warm Lake, gain the divide either by a steep but short snow patch above the lake (early season) or by talus about a quarter mile south of the lake. Turn onto the crest and follow the ridge toward Gilbert, which stays in view most of the way. A plateau-like stretch leads to the base of the summit block. Skirt the cliffs, cross a moderately steep snowfield and a short boulder field, then reach the top through a notch in the buttress by Class 3 rock.
descent_text: Reverse the route. Note landmarks on the way up, because the broad divide is easy to lose in cloud on the return. Cross the snowfield below the summit block with the same care as on the way up.
hazards: Loose rock on the divide and the upper scramble
Snowfield below the summit block, steeper and icier early and late in the season
Brushy, unmarked ground between the trail and Warm Lake
Route-finding on the broad divide in poor visibility
watch_out: The road to the trailhead has been closed for long spells in past years; confirm it is open
The turn-off from the maintained trail to Warm Lake is unsigned
gear: Ice axe in June and early July or after fresh snow
Microspikes or light crampons early and late in the season

road.name: South Fork Tieton / Conrad Meadows road
road.driveNote: Paved but rough, with unannounced bumps near the end; closed for repairs for long periods in past years.

name: Glacier Lake
best_season: August; late July and September are also good when the high basin is snow-free
overview: The east-side scramble to Chikamin Peak. A rough trail climbs Mineral Creek past the Park Lakes to the Pacific Crest Trail. A boot path then drops to Glacier Lake, the usual camp, and the route climbs the basin above it to the southeast slopes and south ridge, finishing with a short Class 3 chimney on the summit horn. Most parties camp at Park Lakes or Glacier Lake; strong parties do it in one very long day.
approach: Park at the Mineral Creek trailhead at the end of the Cooper Lake road. Follow the Mineral Creek trail through old-growth, an old mining road and brushy avalanche clearings, steeply up to Upper Park Lake at about 4 miles, and on to the Pacific Crest Trail at about 5.4 miles (about 2,600 ft of gain). Go west on the PCT to the last switchback before the climb to Chikamin Pass and take the boot path down roughly 600 ft to Glacier Lake.
beta: Skirt Glacier Lake, aim for the tall thin rock above it, and climb through the boulder field (the most common place to lose the way). Bear left toward the largest pond, keep to the right side of the creek on the faint boot path to a tarn near 5,360 ft, then go southwest to a small col. Climb the southeast slopes to the south ridge, follow it to the summit horn, and finish up a short Class 3 chimney (solid, with big holds) and about 75 ft of easy scrambling.
descent_text: Reverse the route. The chimney is short enough to downclimb; the boulder field is where the line back to the lake is hardest to see from above. Allow energy for the 600 ft climb out of the Glacier Lake basin to the PCT at the end of the day.
hazards: Overgrown, brushy trail on Mineral Creek
Stinging insects reported in the creek section
Easy-to-lose boot path in the boulder field
Loose scree and steep heather on the upper slopes
watch_out: The Mineral Creek trail was posted closed for the Three Queens Fire in July 2026; check current status
The route is very long for a day trip
gear: Trekking poles for the brushy approach
what_to_bring: Map and GPS track for the boulder field

road.name: Cooper Lake Road to Mineral Creek
road.driveNote: Paved to Cooper Lake, then gravel; the trailhead is about 3 miles past Cooper Pass at the valley bottom.

name: North Slopes via Blum Lakes
best_season: Mid-July through September for bare ground; April to June is the snow season, popular with ski and snow parties but with cornices and steep snow
overview: The usual way up Hagan: a steep climbers' path to the Blum Lakes, then a glacier-edge and snow route to a saddle among Hagan's peaks, and an exposed Class 3 finish. Hagan is a small range of several summits rather than one peak, so confirm the true high point (the southern one) before the last scramble. Most parties camp at the Blum Lakes and pair it with Mount Blum.
approach: Park at the Baker River trailhead at the end of the Baker Lake road (about 800 ft). Walk the Baker River trail for a few minutes to the Blum Creek bridge, then take the faint, flagged climbers' path up the north side of Blum Creek. It is brushy at first, then steep forest to about 4,500 ft; traverse up and south to a talus field near 4,900 ft and cross to Lower Blum Lake, then follow the path to Upper Blum Lake (about 5,020 ft). Travel off the path is very difficult (devil's club, blueberry, brush). North Cascades National Park rules apply: a backcountry permit and camping limits.
beta: From the lakes, climb toward the ridge to the southeast and gain about 5,600 ft, then turn south and cross the Hagan Glacier, roped if it is crevassed, to the saddle between the southern and middle peaks. Drop a short way into the Berdeen Lake drainage if the snow is good, and climb steep snow to the summit block. The block is exposed Class 3 with a few Class 4 moves; about ten minutes of rock above the col.
descent_text: Reverse the route. The descent takes as long as the ascent; the path below the lakes is easy to lose, and the Blum Creek crossing gets harder once the snow bridge melts.
hazards: Crevasses and a moat on the Hagan Glacier
Steep snow and cornices on the ridge in spring and early summer
Exposed Class 3-4 rock on the summit block
Dense brush and an easily lost path below the lakes

name: Northwest Ridge
best_season: Mid-July to September, once the snow has left the upper ridge; May to June trips meet snow above about 6,000-7,000 ft.
overview: A pathless climb from the Stuart Lake trailhead up the west side of Cannon: brush and boulders to a high basin, then the northwest ridge, finishing with a short friction slab onto the summit block.
approach: From the Stuart Lake trailhead (about 3,400 ft; Northwest Forest Pass) take the Stuart Lake trail about 1.25 miles to just before the Mountaineer Creek bridge, then leave the trail and go up west and south through open forest.
beta: Boulder field and waterfall gully near 4,400 ft, a cliff band near 5,200 ft scrambled on grass and trees, a flat basin near 6,100 ft, then northeast on rock and grass to the ridge near 7,400 ft. The upper ridge follows vegetated ledges at class 3; boulder-only lines are usually off route. The summit block is a friction slab of roughly 15 ft.
descent_text: Most parties retrace the route; a longer alternative heads east across the Druid Plateau, over Prusik Pass, through the Enchantments and down Aasgard Pass.
hazards: steep brush and slide alder low on the mountain
snow and ice on the upper ridge into July
exposed friction slab at the summit, dangerous when wet or icy

name: East Face
best_season: July to September once the Harts Pass road is open and the east slopes are mostly snow-free; October trips meet fresh snow on the face.
overview: The approach most climbers use: a bushwhack from the Slate Creek road to the east ridge, a steep vegetated slot, scrambling into the east cirque, then a ledge traverse to the summit gully on the west side of the top block.
approach: Drive the Harts Pass road over the pass and down the Slate Creek road to the locked gate (about 3,800 ft). Walk the old South Fork Slate Creek road roughly a mile to the large bridge near 4,000 ft, then leave the road and travel south through open forest.
beta: Aim for the big talus field right at 4,900 ft to limit slide-alder fighting, keep left through the forest to the next boulder field, gain the east ridge bench near 6,200 ft, climb the steep grassy slot (class 4) and follow the ridge at class 2-3 into the east cirque. From the saddle near 8,150 ft traverse ledges to the summit gully; the last pitch is a short corner or slot at class 3-4, with a low-fifth variation on the north side.
descent_text: Retrace the route; descend the green slot carefully and keep to the forest on the left on the way down to avoid the alder.
hazards: loose rock in the slot and cirque
steep slide alder on the approach
exposed ledges near the summit block
wet snow on the face in May and October

name: North Ridge
best_season: July through September, when the ridge is free of snow
overview: The north ridge is the rock route on Whistler, climbed from the highway shoulder shared with Cutthroat Peak. A climbers' trail drops into the open basin between the two peaks, then the route follows the ridge to the summit pyramid, mostly class 3 with some class 4 steps, over about 2,700 ft of gain. The ridge is exposed in places, and a fall would have serious consequences.
beta: Pick up the climbers' trail from the pullout, cross the basin and gain the notch between Whistler and Cutthroat. Follow the north ridge, which dips slightly in places, to the summit pyramid. There the rock opens into many possible lines; keeping to the north (right-hand) side is easier, and there are rappel slings on the far side. Expect loose rock and choose lines carefully.
approach: Park on the wide paved shoulder of SR-20 about three quarters of a mile west of the signed Blue Lake trailhead lot, on the north side, where there is no guard rail. A good climbers' trail leads from the road through forest into the basin. No pass is needed at the pullout; the Blue Lake lot needs a forest pass.
descent_text: Retrace the ridge. A short loose step is usually rappelled instead of downclimbed.
turnaround: If the rock above the notch is wet or iced, or storms build in the afternoon, turn back at the ridge.
hazards: Loose rock on the ridge and summit pyramid
Exposed ridge: a fall would be serious

road.name: SR-20 (North Cascades Highway)
road.driveNote: SR-20 closes for winter, normally from about mid-November to mid-April.

name: Northwest Route
approach: Take the Dingford Creek trail about 2.2 miles to its crossing of Goat Creek (about 2,600 ft). Leave the trail, cross the valley southward, and enter the basin that holds Price Lake.
beta: Four cliff bands cross the way, near 2,800, 3,200, 3,600 and 4,500 ft; each goes with careful map reading, and the slopes between are talus or forest. Keep east of the creek draining Price Lake. In snow the gully above the lake is wide and steady. Roughly 4,100 ft of gain over about 4 miles, 4 to 6 hours up. Inside the Alpine Lakes Wilderness.
